claim: The characteristics of pneumococcal carriage vary between infants and adults.
source: The characteristics of pneumococcal carriage vary between infants and adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Host immune factors have been shown to contribute to age-specific differences in pneumococcal carriage.
source: Host immune factors have been shown to contribute to these age-specific differences, but the role of pathogen sequence variation is currently less well-known.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to existing literature on host immune factors.

claim: The role of pathogen sequence variation in age-specific differences in pneumococcal carriage is currently less well-known.
source: Host immune factors have been shown to contribute to these age-specific differences, but the role of pathogen sequence variation is currently less well-known.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Age-dependent colonization showed weak evidence of being heritable in the Dutch cohort (h2 = 0.10, 95% CI 0.00–0.69).
source: Age-dependent colonization showed weak evidence of being heritable in the first cohort (h2 = 0.10, 95% CI 0.00–0.69) and stronger evidence in the second cohort (h2 = 0.56, 95% CI 0.23–0.87).
evidence: This is a direct result from heritability analysis performed on the Dutch cohort data.

claim: Age-dependent colonization showed stronger evidence of being heritable in the Maela cohort (h2 = 0.56, 95% CI 0.23–0.87).
source: Age-dependent colonization showed weak evidence of being heritable in the first cohort (h2 = 0.10, 95% CI 0.00–0.69) and stronger evidence in the second cohort (h2 = 0.56, 95% CI 0.23–0.87).
evidence: This is a direct result from heritability analysis performed on the Maela cohort data.

claim: Serotypes explained a proportion of the heritability in the Dutch cohort (h2serotype = 0.07, 95% CI 0.04–0.14).
source: We found that serotypes and genetic background (strain) explained a proportion of the heritability in the first cohort (h2serotype = 0.07, 95% CI 0.04–0.14 and h2GPSC = 0.06, 95% CI 0.03–0.13) and the second cohort (h2serotype = 0.11, 95% CI 0.05–0.21 and h2GPSC = 0.20, 95% CI 0.12–0.31).
evidence: This is a direct result from heritability analysis of serotype data in the Dutch cohort.

claim: Genetic background (strain) explained a proportion of the heritability in the Dutch cohort (h2GPSC = 0.06, 95% CI 0.03–0.13).
source: We found that serotypes and genetic background (strain) explained a proportion of the heritability in the first cohort (h2serotype = 0.07, 95% CI 0.04–0.14 and h2GPSC = 0.06, 95% CI 0.03–0.13) and the second cohort (h2serotype = 0.11, 95% CI 0.05–0.21 and h2GPSC = 0.20, 95% CI 0.12–0.31).
evidence: This is a direct result from heritability analysis of strain data in the Dutch cohort.

claim: Serotypes explained a proportion of the heritability in the Maela cohort (h2serotype = 0.11, 95% CI 0.05–0.21).
source: We found that serotypes and genetic background (strain) explained a proportion of the heritability in the first cohort (h2serotype = 0.07, 95% CI 0.04–0.14 and h2GPSC = 0.06, 95% CI 0.03–0.13) and the second cohort (h2serotype = 0.11, 95% CI 0.05–0.21 and h2GPSC = 0.20, 95% CI 0.12–0.31).
evidence: This is a direct result from heritability analysis of serotype data in the Maela cohort.

claim: Genetic background (strain) explained a proportion of the heritability in the Maela cohort (h2GPSC = 0.20, 95% CI 0.12–0.31).
source: We found that serotypes and genetic background (strain) explained a proportion of the heritability in the first cohort (h2serotype = 0.07, 95% CI 0.04–0.14 and h2GPSC = 0.06, 95% CI 0.03–0.13) and the second cohort (h2serotype = 0.11, 95% CI 0.05–0.21 and h2GPSC = 0.20, 95% CI 0.12–0.31).
evidence: This is a direct result from heritability analysis of strain data in the Maela cohort.

claim: A candidate association (p=1.2 × 10-9) was found upstream of an accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin in a meta-analysis of the cohorts.
source: In a meta-analysis of these cohorts, we found one candidate association (p=1.2 × 10-9) upstream of an accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin.
evidence: This is a direct result from the genome-wide association meta-analysis.

claim: There is a small effect of pathogen genome variation on pneumococcal carriage between child and adult hosts.
source: Overall, while we did find a small effect of pathogen genome variation on pneumococcal carriage between child and adult hosts, this was variable between populations and does not appear to be caused by strong effects of individual genes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the heritability and GWAS analyses performed.

claim: The effect of pathogen genome variation on pneumococcal carriage between child and adult hosts was variable between populations.
source: Overall, while we did find a small effect of pathogen genome variation on pneumococcal carriage between child and adult hosts, this was variable between populations and does not appear to be caused by strong effects of individual genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the different heritability estimates between the Dutch and Maela cohorts.

claim: The effect of pathogen genome variation on pneumococcal carriage between child and adult hosts does not appear to be caused by strong effects of individual genes.
source: Overall, while we did find a small effect of pathogen genome variation on pneumococcal carriage between child and adult hosts, this was variable between populations and does not appear to be caused by strong effects of individual genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of strong individual gene associations in the GWAS.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common commensal of the human upper respiratory tract and nasopharynx.
source: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common commensal of the human upper respiratory tract and nasopharynx, but can also cause pneumonia and invasive diseases such as sepsis or meningitis (Bogaert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bogaert et al., 2004.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause pneumonia and invasive diseases such as sepsis or meningitis.
source: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common commensal of the human upper respiratory tract and nasopharynx, but can also cause pneumonia and invasive diseases such as sepsis or meningitis (Bogaert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bogaert et al., 2004.

claim: Invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) has a high mortality.
source: Invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) has a high mortality, and the overall mortality rate from IPD is higher in extreme age ranges, such as infants and the elderly (Wahl et al., 2018; O Brien et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wahl et al., 2018 and O Brien et al., 2009.

claim: The overall mortality rate from IPD is higher in extreme age ranges, such as infants and the elderly.
source: Invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) has a high mortality, and the overall mortality rate from IPD is higher in extreme age ranges, such as infants and the elderly (Wahl et al., 2018; O Brien et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wahl et al., 2018 and O Brien et al., 2009.

claim: In the Netherlands, pneumococcal carriage rates are higher in children than in adults, with a prevalence of up to 80% at 2 years of age.
source: In the Netherlands, pneumococcal carriage rates are higher in children than in adults, with a prevalence of up to 80% at 2 years of age (Wyllie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wyllie et al., 2016.

claim: Host age is known to affect carriage prevalence and carriage duration of different serotypes.
source: Host age is known to affect carriage prevalence and carriage duration of different serotypes (Stearns et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2012b), which is suggested to be driven by differences in immunity.(Wyllie et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stearns et al., 2015 and Turner et al., 2012b.

claim: Age-dependent differences in carriage prevalence and duration are suggested to be driven by differences in immunity.
source: Host age is known to affect carriage prevalence and carriage duration of different serotypes (Stearns et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2012b), which is suggested to be driven by differences in immunity.(Wyllie et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wyllie et al., 2020.

claim: Studies in mice and humans showed evidence for age-dependent host–pathogen interactions involving interleukin (IL)-1 response in reaction to the pore-forming pneumolysin (ply) toxin.
source: Studies in mice and humans showed evidence for age-dependent host–pathogen interactions involving interleukin (IL)-1 response in reaction to the pore-forming pneumolysin (ply) toxin (Kuipers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuipers et al., 2018.

claim: IgA secretion is important in clearing S. pneumoniae from host upper respiratory tract mucosa.
source: IgA secretion is important in clearing S. pneumoniae from host upper respiratory tract mucosa, and this secretion is more effective in previously exposed individuals, the adults (Binsker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Binsker et al., 2020.

claim: IgA secretion is more effective in clearing S. pneumoniae in previously exposed individuals (adults).
source: IgA secretion is important in clearing S. pneumoniae from host upper respiratory tract mucosa, and this secretion is more effective in previously exposed individuals, the adults (Binsker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Binsker et al., 2020.

claim: Bacterial genetics has been shown to explain over 60% of the variability in carriage duration.
source: Bacterial genetics has been shown to explain over 60% of the variability in carriage duration, and specifically that the presence of a bacteriophage inserted in a mediator of genomic competence was associated with a decreased carriage duration (Lees et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lees et al., 2017b.

claim: The presence of a bacteriophage inserted in a mediator of genomic competence was associated with a decreased carriage duration.
source: Bacterial genetics has been shown to explain over 60% of the variability in carriage duration, and specifically that the presence of a bacteriophage inserted in a mediator of genomic competence was associated with a decreased carriage duration (Lees et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lees et al., 2017b.

claim: Pneumococci display over 100 diverse capsular serotypes.
source: Pneumococci are highly genetically variable, displaying over 100 diverse capsular serotypes (Ganaie et al., 2020), which are a major antigen and the strongest predictor of carriage prevalence (Croucher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ganaie et al., 2020.

claim: Capsular serotypes are a major antigen and the strongest predictor of carriage prevalence.
source: Pneumococci are highly genetically variable, displaying over 100 diverse capsular serotypes (Ganaie et al., 2020), which are a major antigen and the strongest predictor of carriage prevalence (Croucher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Croucher et al., 2018.

claim: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs), targeting up to 13 capsule serotypes with high burden of invasive disease, decrease the rate of nasopharyngeal carriage and invasive disease.
source: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs), targeting up to 13 capsule serotypes with high burden of invasive disease, decrease the rate of nasopharyngeal carriage and invasive disease (Whitney et al., 2003; Poehling et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Whitney et al., 2003 and Poehling et al., 2006.

claim: Vaccination with a PCV reduces the disease burden in the target population (young children).
source: Besides a direct effect of vaccination with a PCV on the disease burden in the target population, that is, young children, it also reduces the disease burden caused by pneumococci with vaccine serotypes in the population not eligible for vaccination through indirect protection from colonization – reducing carriage rates in children reduces overall transmission of the most invasive serotypes (Croucher et al., 2018; Desai et al., 2015; von Gottberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Croucher et al., 2018; Desai et al., 2015; von Gottberg et al., 2014.

claim: PCV vaccination reduces the disease burden caused by pneumococci with vaccine serotypes in the population not eligible for vaccination through indirect protection from colonization.
source: Besides a direct effect of vaccination with a PCV on the disease burden in the target population, that is, young children, it also reduces the disease burden caused by pneumococci with vaccine serotypes in the population not eligible for vaccination through indirect protection from colonization – reducing carriage rates in children reduces overall transmission of the most invasive serotypes (Croucher et al., 2018; Desai et al., 2015; von Gottberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Croucher et al., 2018; Desai et al., 2015; von Gottberg et al., 2014.

claim: The introduction of PCV has resulted in the replacement of serotypes not covered by the vaccine.
source: However, the introduction of PCV has resulted in the replacement of serotypes not covered by the vaccine (Croucher et al., 2013; Corander et al., 2017), which in some countries reaches levels of invasive disease return towards pre-vaccine levels (Ladhani et al., 2018; Koelman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Croucher et al., 2013 and Corander et al., 2017.

claim: In some countries, serotype replacement reaches levels of invasive disease return towards pre-vaccine levels.
source: However, the introduction of PCV has resulted in the replacement of serotypes not covered by the vaccine (Croucher et al., 2013; Corander et al., 2017), which in some countries reaches levels of invasive disease return towards pre-vaccine levels (Ladhani et al., 2018; Koelman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ladhani et al., 2018 and Koelman et al., 2020.

claim: The Dutch cohort was made up of 1329 S. pneumoniae isolates comprising 41 unique serotypes.
source: The Dutch cohort was made up of 1329 S. pneumoniae isolates comprising 41 unique serotypes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Dutch cohort.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, 689 (52%) isolates comprised seven serotypes: 19A (225; 17%), 11A (111; 8%), 6C (97; 7%), 23B (84; 6%), 10A (67; 5%), 16F (54; 4%), and 21 (51; 4%).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Dutch cohort.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, a minority of isolates (101; 8%) belonged to one of the vaccine serotypes.
source: In this cohort of which the children were vaccinated, a minority of isolates (101; 8%) belonged to one of the vaccine serotypes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Dutch cohort.

claim: A total of 3085 pneumococcal isolates of the Maela cohort comprised 64 unique serotype groups.
source: A total of 3085 pneumococcal isolates of the Maela (unvaccinated) cohort comprised 64 unique serotype groups (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Maela cohort.

claim: In the Maela cohort, 1631 (53%) isolates comprised five serotypes: non-typable (511; 17%), 19F (402, 13%), 23F (307, 10%), 6B (236; 8%), and 14 (175; 6%).
source: Of these isolates, 1631 (53%) comprised five serotypes: non-typable (511; 17%), 19F (402, 13%), 23F (307, 10%), 6B (236; 8%), and 14 (175; 6%).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Maela cohort.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, there were 59 unique sequence clusters of which the four largest were GPSC 4 (171; 13%), GPSC 3 (156; 12%), GPSC 7 (131; 10%), and GPSC 11 (119; 9%).
source: In the Dutch cohort, there were 59 unique sequence clusters of which the four largest sequence clusters were GPSC 4 (171; 13%), GPSC 3 (156; 12%), GPSC 7 (131; 10%), and GPSC 11 (119; 9%) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Dutch cohort.

claim: There were 127 unique sequence clusters found in the Maela cohort.
source: There were 127 unique sequence clusters found in the Maela cohort (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Maela cohort.

claim: The four largest sequence clusters in the Maela cohort were GPSC 1 (352; 13%), GPSC 28 (190; 7%), GPSC 20 (168; 6%), and GPSC 42 (123; 5%).
source: The four largest sequence clusters were GPSC 1 (352; 13%), GPSC 28 (190; 7%), GPSC 20 (168; 6%), and GPSC 42 (123; 5%).
evidence: This is a direct count from the sequenced samples in the Maela cohort.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C was overrepresented in children relative to adults (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing).
source: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing) and serotype 15B (p=0.02) were overrepresented in children relative to adults, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5), while in the Maela cohort, serotype groups overrepresented in children were serotype 23F (chi-squared test, p=0.04) and serotype 6B (chi-squared test, p=0.04); while non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing serotype frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 15B was overrepresented in children relative to adults (p=0.02).
source: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing) and serotype 15B (p=0.02) were overrepresented in children relative to adults, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5), while in the Maela cohort, serotype groups overrepresented in children were serotype 23F (chi-squared test, p=0.04) and serotype 6B (chi-squared test, p=0.04); while non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing serotype frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5).
source: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing) and serotype 15B (p=0.02) were overrepresented in children relative to adults, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5), while in the Maela cohort, serotype groups overrepresented in children were serotype 23F (chi-squared test, p=0.04) and serotype 6B (chi-squared test, p=0.04); while non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing serotype frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Maela cohort, serotype 23F was overrepresented in children (chi-squared test, p=0.04).
source: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing) and serotype 15B (p=0.02) were overrepresented in children relative to adults, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5), while in the Maela cohort, serotype groups overrepresented in children were serotype 23F (chi-squared test, p=0.04) and serotype 6B (chi-squared test, p=0.04); while non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing serotype frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Maela cohort, serotype 6B was overrepresented in children (chi-squared test, p=0.04).
source: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing) and serotype 15B (p=0.02) were overrepresented in children relative to adults, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5), while in the Maela cohort, serotype groups overrepresented in children were serotype 23F (chi-squared test, p=0.04) and serotype 6B (chi-squared test, p=0.04); while non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing serotype frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Maela cohort, non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4).
source: In the Dutch cohort, serotype 6C (chi-squared test, p=0.02, not corrected for multiple testing) and serotype 15B (p=0.02) were overrepresented in children relative to adults, serotype 3 was overrepresented in adults relative to children (p=2.5 × 10–5), while in the Maela cohort, serotype groups overrepresented in children were serotype 23F (chi-squared test, p=0.04) and serotype 6B (chi-squared test, p=0.04); while non-typeable serogroup was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=3.0 × 10–4) (Table 1).

claim: None of the 20 largest groups of sequence clusters overlapped between the cohorts.
source: None of the 20 largest groups of sequence clusters overlapped between the cohorts.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the sequence cluster distributions between cohorts.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, only GPSC 11 was significantly associated with carriage in children (chi-squared test, p=0.03, not corrected for multiple testing).
source: In the Dutch cohort, only GPSC 11 was significantly associated with carriage in children (chi-squared test, p=0.03, not corrected for multiple testing), while GPSC 12 (chi-squared test, p=1.2 × 10–4) and GPSC 38 (chi-squared test, p=2.1 × 10–4) were overrepresented in adults.
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing strain frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, GPSC 12 was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=1.2 × 10–4).
source: In the Dutch cohort, only GPSC 11 was significantly associated with carriage in children (chi-squared test, p=0.03, not corrected for multiple testing), while GPSC 12 (chi-squared test, p=1.2 × 10–4) and GPSC 38 (chi-squared test, p=2.1 × 10–4) were overrepresented in adults.
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing strain frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, GPSC 38 was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=2.1 × 10–4).
source: In the Dutch cohort, only GPSC 11 was significantly associated with carriage in children (chi-squared test, p=0.03, not corrected for multiple testing), while GPSC 12 (chi-squared test, p=1.2 × 10–4) and GPSC 38 (chi-squared test, p=2.1 × 10–4) were overrepresented in adults.
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing strain frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Maela cohort, only sequence cluster GPSC 128 was overrepresented in children compared to adults (chi-squared test, p=0.04).
source: In the Maela cohort, only sequence cluster GPSC 128 was overrepresented in children compared to adults (chi-squared test, p=0.04), while GPSC 20 (chi-squared test, p=7.0 × 10–3) and GPSC 74 (chi-squared test, p=0.04) were overrepresented in adults (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing strain frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Maela cohort, GPSC 20 was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=7.0 × 10–3).
source: In the Maela cohort, only sequence cluster GPSC 128 was overrepresented in children compared to adults (chi-squared test, p=0.04), while GPSC 20 (chi-squared test, p=7.0 × 10–3) and GPSC 74 (chi-squared test, p=0.04) were overrepresented in adults (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing strain frequencies between age groups.

claim: In the Maela cohort, GPSC 74 was overrepresented in adults (chi-squared test, p=0.04).
source: In the Maela cohort, only sequence cluster GPSC 128 was overrepresented in children compared to adults (chi-squared test, p=0.04), while GPSC 20 (chi-squared test, p=7.0 × 10–3) and GPSC 74 (chi-squared test, p=0.04) were overrepresented in adults (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on chi-squared test results comparing strain frequencies between age groups.

claim: Pan-genomic variation could be used to predict host age to some degree of accuracy (area under the ROC curve 0.82 [Dutch cohort]; 0.91 [Maela cohort]).
source: In both cohorts, pan-genomic variation could be used to predict host age to some degree of accuracy (area under the receiver-operating characteristic [ROC] curve 0.82 [Dutch cohort]; 0.91 [Maela cohort]), suggestive of some level of heritability and association of host age with strain (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on elastic net prediction models fitted to unitigs, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Prediction between cohorts using a simple linear model failed as the genetic variants chosen as predictors were not found in the other cohort.
source: Prediction between cohorts using a simple linear model failed as the genetic variants chosen as predictors were not found in the other cohort – again highlighting the high level of genetic heterogeneity between cohorts.
evidence: This is based on attempting to use predictors from one cohort to predict age in the other cohort.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, none of the unitigs, SNPs, COGs, or rare variants surpassed the threshold for multiple testing correction.
source: In the Dutch cohort, none of the unitigs, SNPs, COGs, or rare variants surpassed the threshold for multiple testing correction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the GWAS results for the Dutch cohort shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the Maela cohort, unitigs in the ugpA gene surpassed the threshold for statistical significance.
source: In the Maela cohort, unitigs in the ugpA gene surpassed the threshold for statistical significance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but these did not hold after meta-analysis.
evidence: This is based on the GWAS results for the Maela cohort shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unitigs in the ugpA gene that surpassed the threshold for statistical significance in the Maela cohort did not hold after meta-analysis.
source: In the Maela cohort, unitigs in the ugpA gene surpassed the threshold for statistical significance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but these did not hold after meta-analysis.
evidence: This is based on comparing the Maela cohort GWAS results with the meta-analysis results.

claim: After meta-analysis, there were two hits that surpassed the threshold for statistical significance.
source: After meta-analysis, there were two hits that surpassed the threshold for statistical significance (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis GWAS results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The first significant hit is a nucleotide sequence marked by multiple unitigs with the lowest p-value of 1.2 × 10–9.
source: The first is a nucleotide sequence marked by multiple unitigs of which the lowest has a p-value of 1.2 × 10–9 (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis GWAS results.

claim: The significant nucleotide sequence does not map to the S. pneumoniae D39V reference sequence.
source: This sequence does not map to the S. pneumoniae D39V reference sequence (Altschul et al., 1990)
evidence: This is based on mapping the unitigs to the reference genome.

claim: The significant unitigs map in the intergenic region between open-reading frames encoding the accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin and a MarR-like regulator.
source: Upon inspection of the individual sequences these unitigs are called from, we find them to map in the intergenic region between open-reading frames encoding the accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin and a MarR-like regulator, respectively.
evidence: This is based on manual inspection of the sequences containing the significant unitigs.

claim: The intergenic region containing the significant unitigs contains sequences resembling transposable elements and an open-reading frame encoding a transposase.
source: This region contains sequences resembling transposable elements and an open-reading frame encoding a transposase.
evidence: This is based on annotation of the region containing the significant unitigs.

claim: The significant unitigs map upstream of the start codon of the accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin.
source: The unitigs map upstream of the start codon of the accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin.
evidence: This is based on mapping the unitigs relative to gene positions.

claim: The significant sequence is present in 169 out of 1282 (13%) sequences in the Dutch cohort and in 241 out of 3085 (8%) in the Maela cohort.
source: The sequence is present in 169 out of 1282 (13%) sequences in the Dutch cohort and in 241 out of 3085 (8%) in the Maela cohort.
evidence: This is based on counting the presence of the sequence across samples in both cohorts.

claim: The significant sequence is present in isolates dispersed over the phylogenetic tree and associated with carriage in children.
source: The sequence is present in isolates dispersed over the phylogenetic tree and associated with carriage in children (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on mapping the sequence presence onto the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The accessory Sec-dependent serine-rich glycoprotein adhesin protein is involved in adhesion to epithelial cells and biofilm formation.
source: This protein is involved in adhesion to epithelial cells and biofilm formation (Chan et al., 2020; Middleton et al., 2021; Weiser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2020; Middleton et al., 2021; Weiser et al., 2018.

claim: Variation of the sequence upstream of the Sec-dependent adhesin protein start codon may alter the expression of the protein and affect carriage.
source: Given that this sequence lies just upstream of the start codon, it is plausible that variation of this sequence alters the expression of the Sec-dependent adhesin protein, and therefore affects carriage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the association finding based on the location of the variant.

claim: The second significant hit is a burden of rare variants in a gene for tryptophan synthase, trpB, with a p-value of 5.0 × 10–5.
source: The second hit is a burden of rare variants in a gene for tryptophan synthase, trpB, that surpass the threshold for statistical significance at a p-value of 5.0 × 10–5.
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis GWAS results for rare variant burden.

claim: The trpB variants are two frameshift variants of very low frequency.
source: The variants are two frameshift variants of very low frequency.
evidence: This is based on annotation of the rare variants in trpB.

claim: The trpB frameshift variants result in a predicted dysfunctional trpB gene in 9 out of 1282 (1%) sequences in the Dutch cohort and in 12 out of 3073 (0.4%) sequences in the Maela cohort.
source: These result in a predicted dysfunctional trpB gene in 9 out of 1282 (1%) sequences in the Dutch cohort and in 12 out of 3073 (0.4%) sequences in the Maela cohort.
evidence: This is based on counting the presence of the frameshift variants across samples in both cohorts.

claim: The association of the trpB gene is likely to be an artifact of low allele frequency.
source: This association of the trpB gene is likely to be an artifact of low allele frequency as we estimate we are only powered to detect variation in at least 5% of isolates.
evidence: This is an inference based on power calculations and the observed allele frequency.

evidence: This is based on counting pilus gene presence across age groups in the Dutch cohort.

claim: In the Dutch cohort, pilus gene presence was not associated with host age whether or not the genetic background was adjusted for (p=0.35, uncorrected for population structure, and p=0.69, corrected for population structure).

evidence: This is calculated from the heritability estimates for strain (h2GPSC = 0.06) relative to total heritability (h2 = 0.10) in the Dutch cohort.

claim: Some strains and serotypes are more likely to be found in an infant or adult nasopharynx.

evidence: This is an inference from the serotype and strain frequency differences observed between age groups.
